what-is-an-evergreen-fund.title: What Is an Evergreen Fund?
what-is-an-evergreen-fund.meta_description: A plain explanation of evergreen funds, how they differ from interval and tender-offer structures, and what wealthy investors should know before considering one.
what-is-an-evergreen-fund.direct_answer: An evergreen fund is a private investment vehicle with no fixed end date that continuously raises capital and offers periodic, limited opportunities to redeem shares. Unlike a traditional closed-end fund that winds down after a set term, an evergreen fund is built to operate indefinitely, holding illiquid assets like private equity, credit, or real estate.

sections.heading: How It Works
paragraphs: An evergreen fund does not have a maturity date. It raises money on an ongoing basis rather than in a single closing, and it reinvests proceeds from the portfolio instead of returning all capital to investors after a fixed holding period.
This structure lets the fund manager hold long-duration assets without racing against a clock. It also means new investors can typically enter at various points, not just at inception.

sections.heading: Liquidity
paragraphs: Evergreen funds offer periodic liquidity, usually through scheduled repurchase offers at set intervals, such as quarterly. These offers are limited, meaning the fund may cap the amount of capital it repurchases in any given period.
This is different from daily liquidity in public markets. Investors should expect that access to their capital is structured and partial, not immediate or guaranteed.

sections.heading: Costs and Minimums
paragraphs: Fee structures on evergreen funds generally include a management fee based on assets and a performance-based fee tied to gains above a stated threshold. Minimums tend to be higher than public funds, often requiring a substantial initial commitment.
Because the fund is continuously offered, fees and terms can vary by share class or vintage of entry, so investors should read the specific terms of the class they are offered.

sections.heading: Risks
paragraphs: Evergreen funds hold illiquid assets, and the periodic redemption mechanism is not the same as being able to sell on demand. In periods of high redemption requests, the fund may prorate or delay repurchases.

Valuations of private holdings are typically less frequent than public securities and rely on manager estimates. Investors should understand that this structure carries the same underlying market and asset-specific risks as any private investment.

faq.question: Can I redeem my investment in an evergreen fund whenever I want?
faq.answer: No. Redemptions happen only during scheduled repurchase windows, and the fund may limit how much it repurchases in any given period. Your ability to exit depends on the fund's specific terms and current demand for liquidity.

faq.question: Is an evergreen fund the same as a mutual fund?
faq.answer: No. Mutual funds offer daily liquidity and invest primarily in public securities, while evergreen funds hold illiquid private assets and offer only periodic, limited liquidity. The two are structured for very different purposes.

faq.question: Why would a fund choose an evergreen structure instead of a fixed term?
faq.answer: An evergreen structure allows the manager to hold long-duration assets without being forced to sell on a fixed schedule. It also allows the fund to accept new capital continuously rather than only at a single closing.

faq.question: Are evergreen funds only for institutional investors?
faq.answer: Access varies by fund, but many evergreen funds are structured for accredited or qualified investors rather than the general public. Minimums and eligibility requirements differ from fund to fund.

faq.question: What happens if too many investors want to redeem at once?
faq.answer: The fund may prorate the repurchase, meaning each investor receives only a portion of what they requested. This is a structural feature of evergreen funds and something to understand before committing capital.

what-is-an-evergreen-fund.closing: Evergreen funds offer a different liquidity and time horizon than public markets or fixed-term private funds, with tradeoffs that depend on your own goals and cash flow needs, so ask your advisor whether this fits your situation.

how-do-i-protect-my-portfolio-from-a-mar.title: How Evergreen and Interval Funds Fit Into a Portfolio During a Market Downturn
how-do-i-protect-my-portfolio-from-a-mar.meta_description: No fund structure protects a portfolio from a market crash. Here is how evergreen and interval funds behave in downturns, and what to weigh before adding one.
how-do-i-protect-my-portfolio-from-a-mar.direct_answer: No fund structure, including evergreen or interval funds, can protect your portfolio from a market crash or guarantee a particular outcome in a downturn. What these structures can do is offer a different liquidity and valuation pattern than public markets, which changes how a downturn shows up in your portfolio rather than whether it happens.

sections.heading: What Evergreen and Interval Funds Actually Are
paragraphs: Evergreen funds are open-ended vehicles that hold private assets and offer periodic subscriptions and redemptions, often monthly or quarterly, instead of daily trading. Interval funds are a specific regulatory structure that must offer to repurchase a set percentage of shares at set intervals, typically quarterly.

Both structures exist to let investors hold less liquid assets, like private credit, real estate, or private equity, inside a fund that still has some redemption mechanism. That mechanism is limited by design and is not the same as being able to sell whenever you want.

sections.heading: How They Behave During a Downturn
paragraphs: Because the underlying assets are not traded daily, evergreen and interval funds do not get repriced by public markets every minute. Their valuations typically come from periodic appraisals or models, which means reported values can lag what is happening in public markets during a fast selloff.

This lag is often misread as stability. It is not protection or reduced risk. It simply means the impact of a downturn may show up later, and possibly all at once, rather than in real time. Redemption requests can also increase sharply during stress, and funds are permitted to gate or limit redemptions when that happens, which can leave you holding the position longer than planned.

sections.heading: Costs, Minimums, and Access
paragraphs: These funds generally carry higher minimums than public mutual funds or ETFs, often in the tens of thousands of dollars or more, and are typically limited to accredited investors or qualified clients. Fee structures usually include a management fee and sometimes a performance-based component, along with fund-level expenses tied to the private assets held.

Because of gating provisions and appraisal-based pricing, these are not tools for accessing cash quickly in an emergency. They are long-horizon allocations that should be sized with that illiquidity in mind.

sections.heading: Where This Fits in Diversification
paragraphs: Diversification means holding assets that do not all respond to the same triggers in the same way at the same time. Adding private market exposure through an evergreen or interval fund can broaden that set of triggers, but it introduces its own risks: illiquidity, valuation lag, manager concentration, and redemption limits.

This is a structural tradeoff, not a hedge. Whether it makes sense depends on your time horizon, your need for liquidity, and how much of your portfolio is already tied to public market swings. For a broader look at how these structures compare, see our Index of evergreen, interval, and tender-offer funds.

faq.question: Can any fund guarantee protection from a market crash?
faq.answer: No. Every fund structure carries risk, and none can guarantee a particular outcome during a market downturn. Claims of guaranteed protection should be treated as a red flag.

faq.question: Why don't evergreen fund values drop right away when markets fall?
faq.answer: Their valuations are typically based on periodic appraisals rather than daily market pricing, so reported values can lag public markets. This is a timing difference in reporting, not evidence that the underlying assets are insulated from the same economic pressures.

faq.question: What happens if I want to redeem during a crash?
faq.answer: Evergreen and interval funds can limit or gate redemptions during periods of high demand, meaning you may not get full or immediate access to your capital. This is a structural feature of these funds and should be assumed as a real possibility, not an edge case.

faq.question: Are interval funds safer than evergreen funds?
faq.answer: They are different, not safer. Interval funds have a regulatory requirement to offer repurchases at set intervals, which creates a predictable schedule, but the repurchase amount is still capped and not guaranteed to meet demand.

faq.question: How much of my portfolio should go into these structures?
faq.answer: There is no universal answer, since it depends on your liquidity needs, time horizon, and existing exposure to public markets. This is a sizing and planning decision that should be made with a full view of your financial picture.

how-do-i-protect-my-portfolio-from-a-mar.closing: Evergreen and interval funds change how illiquidity and valuation work in a portfolio, but they do not remove market risk or promise a particular outcome in a downturn. Given the tradeoffs involved, ask your advisor whether this fits your situation.
